metadata.summary: This consensus document addresses ovarian cancer pathology and molecular biology, early-stage disease and pelvic masses during pregnancy, advanced disease, and recurrence. It presents recommendations that achieved consensus on diagnosis, surgery, systemic treatment, maintenance therapy, supportive care and follow-up, alongside voting results. Older or frail patients and people seeking fertility preservation are also considered.

target_population: Patients with newly diagnosed or recurrent tubo-ovarian carcinoma
Pregnant women with adnexal masses or ovarian carcinoma
Young women with ovarian carcinoma who wish to preserve fertility
Older or frail patients with tubo-ovarian carcinoma
Patients with STIC detected during risk-reducing surgery

therapies_index.name: paclitaxel
approved_indications: May be administered during pregnancy when chemotherapy is needed after the first trimester.
May be combined with bevacizumab for recurrent disease in patients who have not previously received bevacizumab.

therapies_index.name: bevacizumab
approved_indications: Recommended with chemotherapy and subsequently as maintenance for newly diagnosed tubo-ovarian carcinoma, irrespective of biomarker status.
May be used again with platinum-based treatment in patients previously given bevacizumab as first-line therapy.
May be added to weekly paclitaxel, PLD or topotecan for recurrent disease if bevacizumab has not previously been given.
therapies_index.administration: With platinumepaclitaxel ChT and then as maintenance for a maximum of 15 months in the first-line setting.
monitoring: Carefully monitor toxicity and concomitant medications when offered to older patients.

therapies_index.name: olaparib
approved_indications: Recommended, alone or with bevacizumab, as maintenance for eligible patients in CR/PR/NED after platinum-based ChT.
therapies_index.administration: Maintenance for 2 years in patients in CR/PR/NED after platinum-based ChT.

therapies_index.name: niraparib
approved_indications: FDA and EMA approved as maintenance monotherapy for BRCA-wt HRD-negative tumours.
May follow platinum-based ChT in eligible patients with HGSC/high-grade EC who achieve CR/PR/NED.
therapies_index.administration: Maintenance for 3 years in patients in CR/PR/NED after platinum-based ChT.

therapies_index.name: rucaparib
approved_indications: EMA approved as maintenance monotherapy for BRCA-wt HRD-negative tumours.
May follow platinum-based ChT in eligible patients with HGSC/high-grade EC who achieve CR/PR/NED.
therapies_index.administration: Maintenance for 2 years in patients in CR/PR/NED after platinum-based ChT.

therapies_index.name: PLD
approved_indications: May be combined with bevacizumab in recurrent disease if bevacizumab has not previously been given.
May be combined with trabectedin for patients intolerant of platinum who relapse after 6 months from their last platinum dose.

therapies_index.name: topotecan
approved_indications: May be combined with bevacizumab in recurrent disease if bevacizumab has not previously been given.

therapies_index.name: trabectedin
approved_indications: May be combined with PLD for patients intolerant of platinum who relapse after 6 months from their last platinum dose.

therapies_index.name: trametinib
approved_indications: Should be considered for relapsed LGSC after platinum failure.

therapies_index.name: paclitaxelecarboplatin ChT
approved_indications: Recommended for LGSC, with or without bevacizumab.
Standard chemotherapy regimen for older or frail patients with tubo-ovarian carcinoma.
therapies_index.administration: Every 3 weeks when used as the standard regimen for older or frail patients.

therapies_index.name: continuous weekly paclitaxel 60 mg/m2ecarboplatin area under the curve (AUC) 2 schedule
approved_indications: May be considered as an alternative chemotherapy schedule for older or frail patients; it may offer better tolerability and QoL.
therapies_index.administration: Continuous weekly paclitaxel 60 mg/m2 with carboplatin area under the curve (AUC) 2.

therapies_index.name: platinumepaclitaxel ChT
approved_indications: Recommended with bevacizumab before bevacizumab maintenance.

therapies_index.name: carboplatinepegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD)
approved_indications: Preferred chemotherapy partner for bevacizumab in recurrent disease after prior PARPis and without prior bevacizumab.

therapies_index.name: carboplatinePLD
approved_indications: Preferred chemotherapy partner for bevacizumab rechallenge in recurrent disease.

therapies_index.name: weekly paclitaxel and bevacizumab
approved_indications: Preferred combination among the specified bevacizumab-containing non-platinum options for recurrent disease in patients without prior bevacizumab, based on a trial subset analysis.

therapies_index.name: trabectedin and PLD
approved_indications: Could be considered for patients intolerant of platinum who relapse after 6 months from the last platinum dose.

therapies_index.name: platinum-based ChT
approved_indications: Recommended as adjuvant treatment for stage I-II high-grade EC and high-risk stage I-II mucinous ovarian carcinoma.
Recommended as adjuvant treatment for stages IC2, IC3 and II CCC; may be considered for stage IC1 CCC and may be omitted for adequately staged IA or IB CCC.
Recommended when chemotherapy is needed after the first trimester of pregnancy.
Recommended for platinum-eligible recurrent disease after previous bevacizumab and PARPis.
therapies_index.administration: During pregnancy, the recommended dosage is the same as for non-pregnant women, and treatment begins after the first trimester.

therapies_index.name: NACT
approved_indications: With subsequent ICS, a valid alternative in advanced disease when initial complete resection is unlikely and histology is chemosensitive, or when medical conditions make a patient a poor surgical candidate.
May be considered for patients with vulnerability and extensive disease.
therapies_index.administration: Given before ICS in the advanced-disease pathway.

therapies_index.name: PARPis
approved_indications: Recommended, with or without bevacizumab, after platinum-based ChT for eligible patients with HGSC/high-grade EC and BRCA-muts or a positive validated GIS who achieve CR/PR/NED.
Recommended as maintenance after a platinum response in specified recurrent-disease pathways, according to prior targeted treatment and tumour characteristics.
therapies_index.administration: In recurrent disease, maintenance continues until progressive disease or unacceptable toxicity.
monitoring: Monitor according to drug-specific safety recommendations, particularly for late safety issues.
Proactively assess potential side-effects during maintenance treatment.
Carefully monitor toxicity and concomitant medications when offered to older patients.

therapies_index.name: endocrine therapy
approved_indications: An option after ChT for maintenance in stage III and IV LGSC.
Should be considered for relapsed LGSC.

therapies_index.name: non-platinum single-agent systemic therapy
approved_indications: One option, alongside supportive care alone, for patients progressing on platinum-based therapy, relapsing after a short TFI, or unable to receive further platinum because of intolerance.

therapies_index.name: HER2-targeted strategies
approved_indications: Potential strategies for patients with mucinous carcinoma identified through HER2 testing.

therapies_index.name: supportive care
approved_indications: Early supportive care may improve symptoms, QoL and survival.
Supportive care alone should be considered when the expected benefit of ChT is limited.
monitoring: Systematically assess symptoms and QoL during treatment.

therapies_index.name: psycho-oncology
approved_indications: Included among early supportive care services for patients with ovarian carcinoma.

therapies_index.name: social care
approved_indications: Included among early supportive care services for patients with ovarian carcinoma.

therapies_index.name: physiotherapy
approved_indications: Included among early supportive care services for patients with ovarian carcinoma.

therapies_index.name: PCS
approved_indications: Preferred for advanced tubo-ovarian carcinoma when complete resection appears achievable.
Preferred for LGSC when residual disease <1 cm can be achieved.
therapies_index.administration: Initial cytoreductive surgery; surgical candidates proceed to laparotomy with the aim of complete cytoreduction.

therapies_index.name: ICS
approved_indications: Performed after NACT in selected patients with advanced tubo-ovarian carcinoma.

therapies_index.name: fertility-sparing surgery
approved_indications: Its availability should be discussed with young patients who have early-stage ovarian carcinoma; the document describes it as appearing safe for borderline tumours, non-epithelial tumours, low-grade stage IA disease and selected IC1 stages.

therapies_index.name: unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with surgical staging
approved_indications: Recommended for young patients wishing to retain fertility when malignancy appears confined to the ovary.

therapies_index.name: minimally invasive surgery
approved_indications: An acceptable fertility-preserving approach if tumour rupture is avoided.
Preferred approach for (re)-staging STIC when feasible.
therapies_index.administration: Avoid tumour rupture when preserving fertility.

therapies_index.name: cryopreservation of gametes
approved_indications: Recommended instead of ovarian tissue cryopreservation for patients wishing to retain fertility.

therapies_index.name: complete surgical resection
approved_indications: Standard surgical approach for stage I-II high-grade EC, CCC and high-risk mucinous ovarian carcinoma.
therapies_index.administration: Includes total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, systematic pelvic and paraaortic lymph node dissection, peritoneal biopsies and cytological analysis.

therapies_index.name: total abdominal hysterectomy
approved_indications: Part of the recommended complete surgical resection for stage I-II high-grade EC, CCC and high-risk mucinous ovarian carcinoma.

therapies_index.name: bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
approved_indications: Part of the recommended complete surgical resection for stage I-II high-grade EC, CCC and high-risk mucinous ovarian carcinoma.

therapies_index.name: omentectomy
approved_indications: Part of the recommended complete surgical resection for stage I-II high-grade EC, CCC and high-risk mucinous ovarian carcinoma.

therapies_index.name: systematic pelvic and paraaortic lymph node dissection
approved_indications: Part of the recommended complete surgical resection for stage I-II high-grade EC, CCC and high-risk mucinous ovarian carcinoma.

therapies_index.name: resection of peritoneal and omental disease
approved_indications: Recommended in ovarian SBT with peritoneal implants to permit distinction between invasive and non-invasive implants.

therapies_index.name: removal of all peritoneal implants combined with peritoneal staging
approved_indications: Recommended as standard treatment for early-stage LGSC with non-invasive peritoneal implants.

therapies_index.name: removal of enlarged or suspicious lymph nodes
approved_indications: Recommended in early-stage LGSC with non-invasive peritoneal implants without routine systematic lymphadenectomy.
Recommended in advanced disease to achieve complete resection.

therapies_index.name: staging of the peritoneum
approved_indications: Recommended when STIC is found.

therapies_index.name: hysterectomy
approved_indications: Should be considered in STIC, particularly for patients with a gBRCA1-mut.

therapies_index.name: resection of suspicious or enlarged extra-abdominal lymph nodes
approved_indications: Should be considered if complete macroscopic intra-abdominal resection is achievable, although its survival impact is unclear.

therapies_index.name: resection of isolated parenchymal liver metastases
approved_indications: Should be considered to achieve complete cytoreduction.

therapies_index.name: HIPEC
therapies_index.administration: A cited prospective trial administered HIPEC at ICS in FIGO stage III tubo-ovarian carcinoma; the consensus conference did not agree on its role in this setting.

therapies_index.name: secondary cytoreductive surgery
approved_indications: Patients with tubo-ovarian carcinoma at first relapse >6 months after completing first-line platinum-based ChT should be assessed for this procedure at an experienced gynaecological oncology centre.

therapies_index.name: cytoreductive surgery
approved_indications: Could be offered at subsequent relapses when complete resection appears feasible.

therapies_index.name: palliative surgery
approved_indications: May be indicated for selected patients with mechanical bowel obstruction after conservative measures fail.

Should be offered only after careful consideration when conditions are unfavourable, including rapidly progressive disease without further systemic options, gastric outlet/upper gastrointestinal obstruction or obstruction at multiple levels.
therapies_index.administration: May remove an obstructing tumour or divert the bowel with a stoma; management should involve an MDT.
key_toxicities: High surgical morbidity is reported for intervention in bowel obstruction associated with peritoneally disseminated tubo-ovarian carcinoma.

therapies_index.name: surgical bypass
approved_indications: May be considered for bowel obstruction when conservative pharmacological management fails.

therapies_index.name: stoma formation
approved_indications: May be considered to divert the bowel in selected patients with obstruction after conservative management fails.

therapies_index.name: bowel decompression
approved_indications: May be considered for bowel obstruction when conservative pharmacological management fails.

therapies_index.name: endoscopic stent placements
approved_indications: May be considered for bowel obstruction when conservative pharmacological management fails.

therapies_index.name: percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomies
approved_indications: May be considered for bowel obstruction when conservative pharmacological management fails.

therapies_index.name: infield RT
approved_indications: Should be considered among treatment options for oligometastatic recurrence within an MDT.

therapies_index.name: thermal ablation
approved_indications: Should be considered among treatment options for oligometastatic recurrence within an MDT.

special_populations.population: Pregnant women with an adnexal mass or ovarian carcinoma
special_populations.considerations: Suspicious adnexal masses warrant assessment at a specialist referral centre. Expert US is the recommended initial imaging test, with MRI recommended for masses that remain indeterminate. The role of serum tumour markers is uncertain, and routine beta-human chorionic gonadotropin and alpha-fetoprotein testing is not recommended during pregnancy. Most functional cysts resolve before 16 weeks of gestation, making expectant management reasonable. Patients receiving ChT for ovarian carcinoma require follow-up in high-risk obstetric units.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: When malignancy risk is high, a proactive surgical approach tailored to gestational age is recommended; surgery can be performed during pregnancy, preferably within 22 weeks of gestation. Termination should be considered if advanced-stage tubo-ovarian carcinoma is diagnosed in the first half of pregnancy. When ChT is needed after the first trimester, platinum-based ChT is recommended at the same dosage used for non-pregnant women. Paclitaxel can also be administered.

special_populations.population: Young women who wish to preserve fertility
special_populations.considerations: Fertility-sparing surgery appears safe for patients with borderline tumours, non-epithelial tumours, low-grade stage IA serous, endometrioid or mucinous expansile subtype tumours, and selected IC1 stages. The fertility-sparing option should be discussed with young patients who have early-stage ovarian carcinoma, and women with ovarian carcinoma seeking fertility preservation need care in an oncofertility clinic. Assessment of an adnexal mass by a US expert is recommended; if that expertise is unavailable, IOTA Assessment of Different NEoplasias in the adneXa model (ADNEX) combined with CA-125 is recommended.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For malignancy apparently limited to the ovary, unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with surgical staging is recommended. Minimally invasive surgery is acceptable if tumour rupture is avoided. Biopsy of the unaffected ovary is not recommended unless involvement is suspected. Gamete cryopreservation is recommended in preference to ovarian-tissue cryopreservation.

special_populations.population: Older or frail patients with tubo-ovarian carcinoma
special_populations.considerations: Chronological age alone should not exclude patients from diagnostic procedures, clinical trials or disease-specific treatment. Vulnerability should be assessed in patients 70 years or of any age with at least two comorbidities, preferably with geriatric specialist support when possible; this assessment should not delay treatment. It should address daily functioning, nutrition, psychological well-being, comorbidities and concomitant medications. Older patients are under-represented in clinical trials, and the document reports poorer outcomes in this population.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Primary complete surgery is recommended when feasible after considering vulnerability, surgical complexity and patient motivation. For patients with vulnerability and extensive disease, NACT can be considered instead. Surgery should take place in expert centres with planned surgery, pre-habilitation, intensive post-operative management, enhanced recovery and home care. The standard ChT regimen is paclitaxelecarboplatin every 3 weeks; continuous weekly paclitaxel 60 mg/m2ecarboplatin area under the curve (AUC) 2 can be considered as an alternative that may improve tolerability and QoL. When indicated, PARPis and/or bevacizumab should be offered with careful monitoring of toxicity and concomitant medications.

special_populations.population: Patients with STIC, including those with hereditary predisposition
special_populations.considerations: Following RRBSO, the presence of STIC is associated with an increased subsequent risk of peritoneal carcinoma. Testing for gBRCA1/2-muts and other high-penetrance hereditary genes is mandatory in STIC. SEE-FIM is recommended for RRBSO, and peritoneal staging is recommended when STIC is found.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For STIC, (re)-staging is recommended, preferably by a minimally invasive procedure, while lymphadenectomy is not recommended. Hysterectomy should be considered, particularly for patients with a gBRCA1-mut; if the uterus is retained in these patients, endometrial sampling is recommended. Adjuvant ChT is not recommended for surgically staged STIC.

conditions.name: tubo-ovarian carcinoma
conditions.description: This designation encompasses more than 90% of malignant ovarian tumours and includes epithelial subtypes with differing morphology and molecular characteristics.
conditions.epidemiology: Ovarian cancer is the second-highest cause of death among gynaecological cancers. In Europe in 2020, estimates were 66 693 new cases and 44 053 deaths; more than two-thirds of patients present with advanced disease.

subtypes.name: HGSC
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The most frequent and most lethal tubo-ovarian carcinoma subtype.

subtypes.name: LGSC
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A distinct serous neoplasm with morphology, molecular events and behaviour that differ from HGSC.

subtypes.name: mucinous ovarian carcinoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: HER2 status may help identify candidates for HER2-targeted strategies.

diagnostic_workup.test: Adequate surgical specimen or image-guided biopsy
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the diagnosis and provide treatment-naive tumour material for molecular analysis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The specimen should contain enough tumour cells, preferably 30%.

diagnostic_workup.test: Cell block from peritoneal or pleural effusions
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide material for molecular analysis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When an effusion specimen is available.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It may be used if it contains sufficient tumour cells.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assist diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: These markers must not be used on their own to distinguish benign, borderline and malignant ovarian tumours.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor response to ChT.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Its role in follow-up is less certain.

staging.system: International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO)

prognostic_tools.name: CA-125 KELIM
components: Longitudinal CA-125 measurements over the first 100 days of treatment
prognostic_tools.interpretation: In the neoadjuvant setting, this dynamic measure predicts the likelihood of complete ICS and the risk of subsequent platinum-resistant relapse.

prognostic_tools.name: CRS
components: Histopathological assessment of an omental specimen, preferably, or an adnexal specimen at ICS
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Provides reproducible prognostic information about response to NACT.

follow_up.schedule: No standard follow-up frequency is established. A reasonable approach is assessment every 34 months for the first 2 years and every 6 months during years 3-5; follow-up beyond 5 years is discussed individually. The schedule may be tailored to prognosis and treatment, including maintenance therapy.
recommended_tests: Discuss the option of routine CA-125 monitoring after completion of first-line ChT with the patient.
Consider assessment of QoL and symptoms using validated tools.
Monitor treatment safety according to the drugs used, with particular attention to late safety issues.
long_term_effects: Iatrogenic toxicity may require management during follow-up.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Long-term follow-up by a physician experienced in gynaecological cancer care is recommended. Follow-up addresses recurrence and secondary cancers, QoL, toxicity and supportive-care needs; psycho-oncology, social care, physiotherapy and patient support groups may form part of early supportive care.

conditions.name: HGSC
conditions.description: This serous carcinoma is distinct from LGSC rather than a higher grade of the same tumour. Most cases arise from STIC at the fimbrial end of the fallopian tube.
conditions.epidemiology: HGSC is the most common and most lethal tubo-ovarian carcinoma. Confirmed gBRCA1/2-muts occur in 13%-15% of HGSCs, and somatic BRCA1/2-muts occur in 5%-7% of tumours. Up to 50% of cases are associated with HRD.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish HGSC from LGSC.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a serous carcinoma is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A tumour resembling LGSC morphologically is classified as HGSC if it has aberrant p53 protein expression and/or a TP53 mutation. Difficult cases warrant specialist review and/or molecular testing.

diagnostic_workup.test: Paired box 8, estrogen receptor, WT-1 and p53 IHC
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support classification of a diagnostically sampled suspected serous carcinoma.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At minimum, on diagnostic biopsies with morphological suspicion of HGSC or LGSC.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: p53 IHC findings should be described as ‘wt or normal’ or ‘mutation-type or aberrant’, not as positive or negative.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify whether the primary origin is adnexal or uterine.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When the primary origin of HGSC is uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify germline and/or somatic mutations relevant to treatment decisions.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis, regardless of stage.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Testing requires adequate tumour material and DNA; a germline finding is confirmed using normal cellular material.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform first-line maintenance treatment decisions.

document_sections.heading: ESGOeESMOeESP consensus conference recommendations on ovarian cancer: pathology and molecular biology and early, advanced and recurrent disease5
document_sections.content: The European Society of Gynaecological Oncology, European Society for Medical Oncology and European Society of Pathology convened an ovarian cancer consensus conference on 15-16 June 2022 in Valencia, Spain. Its panel comprised 44 experts in ovarian cancer management and pathology, an ESMO scientific advisor and a methodologist. Four working groups addressed 18 questions concerning pathology and molecular biology, early-stage disease and pelvic masses in pregnancy, advanced disease including older or frail patients, and recurrent disease. They reviewed relevant literature, drafted recommendations, discussed and revised them with the full panel, and voted. The manuscript presents statements that achieved consensus, their voting results and summaries of their supporting evidence.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: Among gynaecological cancers, ovarian cancer is the second-highest cause of death. Europe had an estimated 66 693 new cases and 44 053 deaths in 2020. More than two-thirds of patients present with advanced disease. Diagnosis in young women raises fertility concerns; diagnosis during pregnancy requires consideration of maternal and fetal factors. More than 90% of malignant ovarian tumours are termed tubo-ovarian carcinoma, also called epithelial ovarian cancer. High-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) is its most frequent and most lethal form. Less common epithelial forms with distinct morphology and molecular features include highgrade endometrioid carcinoma (EC), low-grade serous carcinoma (LGSC) and clear-cell carcinoma (CCC). ESGO and ESMO develop guidance to improve cancer care across Europe, while ESP promotes high-quality pathological diagnosis. Following the 2018 ESMOeESGO consensus conference, the societies convened again on 15-16 June 2022 in Valencia, Spain, adding ESP expertise to address emerging or disputed issues. They combined published evidence and clinical experience and used anonymous voting to develop recommendations intended to improve and harmonise care. This manuscript reports recommendations that achieved consensus and their votes; detailed supporting evidence is in the Supplementary Material. For subjects outside its scope, it directs readers to the 2018 ESMOeESGO recommendations, relevant ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines and the ESGO/ISUOG/IOTA/ESGE consensus statement on preoperative ovarian tumour diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: METHODOLOGY
document_sections.content: The conference followed ESMO Standard Operating Procedures for consensus conferences, and declarations of interest were collected and reviewed under ESMO policy. ESGO and ESMO Guidelines Committees identified the need for the meeting. Anna Fagotti, Jonathan Ledermann and Xavier Matias-Guiu chaired it and assigned 41 additional experts, predominantly from Europe with Asian and US representation, to four working groups. B. Davidson and A. Leary chaired pathology and molecular biology; F. Amant and C. Gourley, early-stage disease and pelvic mass in pregnancy; N. Concin and D. Lorusso, advanced disease including older or frail patients; and C. Fotopoulou and A. González-Martin, recurrent disease. F. Planchamp searched Medline® for the working-group topics; reference lists and additional publications identified by group members were also considered. Groups drafted statements from published findings and clinical experience, which the conference chairs reviewed. At the meeting, 40 people were eligible to vote: 3 conference chairs, 8 working-group chairs and 29 other members. Four members unable to attend or vote onsite participated in subsequent voting and authorship. F. Planchamp and C. Sessa did not vote. After working-group discussion, statements were debated and, where needed, amended by the full panel. An adapted ‘Infectious Diseases Society of America-United States Public Health Service Grading System’ supplied levels of evidence and recommendation grades using evidence available as of 14 June 2022. Voting was anonymous; members could abstain because of insufficient expertise or a conflict of interest. The stated consensus criteria were 75% agreement and 20% disagreement; <75% agreement or >20% disagreement did not qualify. Statements without consensus onsite after two voting rounds underwent a post-conference examination of disagreements using modified GRADE methodology. F. Planchamp subsequently checked whether the evidence supported each assigned level and grade, proposing alternatives where necessary. All authors voted anonymously online again on revised grades or levels; those votes are final. All participants approved the manuscript.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: Voting percentages may not total 100% because of rounding.

document_sections.heading: Pathology and molecular biology
document_sections.content: This topic addresses diagnostic molecular testing, biomarkers during treatment and follow-up, the distinction between LGSC and HGSC, and molecular classification of ovarian EC and CCC. Detailed supporting evidence is identified in Supplementary Material Section 1.

document_sections.heading: 1. Which molecular and genomic tests should be carried out at diagnosis as prognostic or predictive markers for high-grade tubo-ovarian carcinoma?
document_sections.content: Molecular analysis requires adequate tumour tissue or a cytology cell block and can detect mutations or guide therapy, including PARPis when BRCA1/2 pathogenic variant mutations (BRCA1/2-muts) are present. BRCA1/2 testing needs sufficient DNA. Confirmed germline BRCA1/2 mutations (gBRCA1/2-muts) occur in 13%-15% of HGSCs; somatic BRCA1/2-muts occur in 5%-7% of tumours. Genomic instability testing in newly diagnosed high-grade non-mucinous tubo-ovarian carcinoma detects impaired homologous recombination repair, which may result from BRCA mutations or other factors, including mutations in homologous recombination repair genes. CA-125 and HE4 are serological aids to diagnosis. Recommendation 1.1 [IV, A]: Prefer an adequate treatment-naive surgical specimen or image-guided tumour biopsy for diagnosis and molecular testing; consensus 100% (41) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 1.2 [IV, B]: Ensure sufficient tumour cells in every sample, preferably 30%; a peritoneal or pleural effusion cell block may be analysed; consensus 97.6% (40) yes, 2.4% (1) no, 0% (0) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 1.3 [I, A]: Test for germline and/or somatic BRCA-mut at diagnosis in high-grade non-mucinous tubo-ovarian carcinoma irrespective of stage; consensus 98% (39) yes, 3% (1) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 1.4 [IV, B]: Routine tumour testing for mutations in nonBRCA homologous recombination genes is unnecessary, although research testing should be encouraged; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 1.5 [I, A]: At diagnosis, perform genomic instability testing in BRCA wild-type (wt) high-grade non-mucinous FIGO stage III-IV tubo-ovarian carcinoma to inform prediction relevant to first-line maintenance choices; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 1.6: Use an instability assay validated in large clinical cohorts [III, B], preferably in phase III trials [I, A]; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 1.7 [IV, A]: No predictive marker of primary platinum or PARPi resistance is validated at diagnosis, so none is currently recommended; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 1.8 [I, E]: Do not recommend population-wide tubo-ovarian carcinoma screening because it does not reduce cancer deaths; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 1.9 [IV, D]: CA-125, whether alone or combined with HE4, must not be the sole means of distinguishing benign, borderline and malignant ovarian tumours; consensus 97.6% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 2.4% (1) abstain (41 voters).

document_sections.heading: 2. What is the role of circulating and tissue biomarkers during treatment and follow-up?
document_sections.content: CA-125 commonly tracks chemotherapy (ChT) response, but its follow-up role is less certain. During neoadjuvant treatment, modelled CA-125 ELIMination rate constant K (KELIM) predicts the chance of complete interval cytoreductive surgery (ICS) and subsequent platinum-resistant recurrence. Histological assessment of omentum yields the ChT response score (CRS), a reproducible prognostic measure of response to neoadjuvant ChT (NACT). Reversion BRCA-muts in tumour tissue or ctDNA mark PARPi resistance; ctDNA applications outside research need further study. Recommendation 2.1 [IV, A]: Discuss optional routine CA-125 monitoring after first-line ChT with the patient; consensus 88% (35) yes, 8% (3) no, 5% (2) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 2.2 [III, B]: Longitudinal CA-125 during the first 100 days permits calculation of prognostic KELIM, and testing may be considered; consensus 78% (31) yes, 13% (5) no, 10% (4) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 2.3 [IV, A]: Do not routinely monitor ctDNA or circulating tumour cells, but encourage their assessment in research; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 2.4 [III, C]: Consider ctDNA testing for reversion mutations in BRCA-mutated tubo-ovarian carcinoma after at least one platinum line if PARPi treatment is an option; consensus 95% (38) yes, 0% (0) no, 5% (2) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 2.5 [III, B]: Assess prognostic CRS at ICS, preferably in omentum or alternatively in an adnexal specimen; consensus 75% (30) yes, 20% (8) no, 5% (2) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 2.6 [III, C]: At recurrence, tumour testing for a reversion mutation may be considered in BRCA-mutated tumours; consensus 93% (37) yes, 5% (2) no, 3% (1) abstain (40 voters).

document_sections.heading: 3. How should LGSC and HGSC be diagnosed?
document_sections.content: Most LGSC begins in the ovary and develops from benign serous or serous borderline tumours (SBTs); most HGSC develops from STIC at the tubal fimbria. Morphology together with p53 IHC distinguishes them. KRAS and BRAF mutations are common in LGSC, while TP53 mutations are ubiquitous in HGSC. Recommendation 3.1 [IV, A]: Treat LGSC and HGSC as distinct neoplasms in morphology, molecular basis and behaviour, not grades of one tumour type; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 3.2 [IV, A]: Combine morphology and p53 IHC for the distinction; seek specialist review and/or molecular testing when diagnosis is difficult; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 3.3 [IV, A]: Classify an LGSC-like tumour as HGSC if p53 expression is aberrant and/or a TP53 mutation is present; consensus 93% (37) yes, 0% (0) no, 8% (3) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 3.4 [III, A]: Apply International Collaboration on Cancer Reporting recommendations when assigning the primary site of extrauterine HGSC; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 3.5 [IV, A]: Use WT-1 staining when adnexal versus uterine origin of HGSC is uncertain; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 3.6 [IV, A]: Report p53 IHC as ‘wt or normal’ or ‘mutation-type or aberrant’, rather than positive or negative; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 3.7 [IV, A]: At minimum, assess paired box 8, estrogen receptor, WT-1 and p53 by IHC in diagnostic biopsies morphologically suspicious for LGSC or HGSC; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 3.8 [IV, C]: Consider HER2 testing in mucinous carcinoma to identify potential candidates for HER2-directed treatment; consensus 95% (38) yes, 3% (1) no, 3% (1) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 3.9 [IV, C]: Consider KRAS and BRAF mutation testing in LGSC to identify potential candidates for targeted treatment; consensus 95% (38) yes, 5% (2) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters).

document_sections.heading: 4. What is the role of molecular classification in ovarian EC and CCC?
document_sections.content: EC and CCC are associated with endometriosis, although tumour growth may completely obscure it. Applying the endometrial carcinoma TCGA-based classification to ovarian EC is prognostically useful; evidence for its role in ovarian CCC is weaker. DNA MMR IHC and/or MSI testing helps detect ovarian EC and CCC related to Lynch syndrome. Recommendation 4.1 [IV, B]: Consider endometrial carcinoma-style TCGA-based molecular classification to stratify ovarian EC; consensus 95% (38) yes, 5% (2) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters). Recommendation 4.2 [IV, D]: Do not use molecular markers for prognosis in ovarian CCC; consensus 90.2% (37) yes, 0% (0) no, 9.8% (4) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 4.3 [II, A]: Perform DNA MMR IHC and/or MSI testing in ovarian EC and CCC; consensus 100% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (40 voters).

document_sections.heading: Early-stage disease and pelvic mass in pregnancy
document_sections.content: This topic covers adnexal masses in pregnancy, fertility preservation, management of early-stage histological subtypes, SBT implants, LGSC implants and incidental STIC or microscopic HGSC. Detailed supporting evidence is identified in Supplementary Material Section 2.

document_sections.heading: 5. How should an adnexal mass be managed in pregnant women?
document_sections.content: Expertise-dependent US and MRI provide first-line detailed locoregional imaging; the usefulness of serum tumour markers remains unclear. Most functional cysts resolve spontaneously before 16 weeks of gestation, making observation reasonable. Surgery can be performed safely during pregnancy, preferably within 22 weeks. Consider terminating a pregnancy if advanced tubo-ovarian carcinoma is diagnosed in its first half; for patients seeking continuation, platinum-based ChT including paclitaxel may be considered. Cited studies report no impairment of organ function or child development after prenatal exposure to maternal ChT. Recommendation 5.1 [V, A]: Refer every pregnant patient with a suspicious adnexal mass to a specialist centre; consensus 95.1% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 4.9% (2) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 5.2 [III, A]: Expert US is the first imaging choice for a pregnancy-associated adnexal mass; consensus 95.1% (39) yes, 2.4% (1) no, 2.4% (1) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 5.3 [IV, A]: Use MRI next to characterise an indeterminate ovarian mass; consensus 92.7% (38) yes, 0% (0) no, 7.3% (3) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 5.4 [IV, E]: Do not routinely use beta-human chorionic gonadotropin or alpha-fetoprotein during pregnancy; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 5.5 [IV, A]: Where malignancy risk is high, take a proactive surgical approach adapted to gestational age; consensus 92.7% (38) yes, 0% (0) no, 7.3% (3) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 5.6 [IV, A]: If needed after the first trimester, give standard platinum-based ChT at the dosage used for non-pregnant women; consensus 97% (38) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 5.7 [IV, B]: Paclitaxel may also be given in pregnancy; consensus 95% (37) yes, 0% (0) no, 5% (2) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 5.8 [IV, A]: Follow pregnant patients receiving ChT for ovarian carcinoma in high-risk obstetric units; consensus 97.6% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 2.4% (1) abstain (41 voters).

document_sections.heading: 6. How should an adnexal mass be managed for women who want to retain their fertility?
document_sections.content: Fertility-sparing surgery appears safe in borderline and non-epithelial tumours, low-grade stage IA serous, endometrioid or expansile mucinous tumours, and selected IC1 disease. Oncofertility clinics are suited to deliver fertility-preservation care using a quality-programme checklist. Recommendation 6.1 [IV, A]: Discuss fertility-sparing surgery with young patients who have early-stage ovarian carcinoma; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 6.2 [V, A]: Manage patients seeking fertility preservation through an oncofertility clinic; consensus 97% (38) yes, 3% (1) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 6.3 [III, A]: Prefer an expert's subjective US assessment; if unavailable, combine the IOTA Assessment of Different NEoplasias in the adneXa model (ADNEX) with CA-125 to distinguish benign, borderline, early-stage or advanced ovarian carcinoma and secondary carcinomas in young women seeking fertility preservation; consensus 90% (35) yes, 8% (3) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 6.4 [III, A]: Use unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with surgical staging for young patients whose malignancy appears restricted to the ovary and who seek fertility preservation; consensus 95% (37) yes, 3% (1) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 6.5 [IV, A]: Minimally invasive surgery is acceptable if tumour rupture is avoided; consensus 95% (37) yes, 5% (2) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 6.6 [V, E]: Do not biopsy an apparently unaffected ovary unless involvement is suspected; consensus 97% (38) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 6.7 [V, A]: Prefer gamete over ovarian-tissue cryopreservation; consensus 97% (38) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters).

document_sections.heading: 7. How should high-grade EC, CCC and high-risk mucinous stage I-II tubo-ovarian carcinomas be managed?
document_sections.content: Lymph-node resection remains debated for these histologies, with retrospective evidence. Generally, nodal metastasis risk is 20% in stage I and 40% in stage II, although reported values differ with grade and histology: 17.4% for early-stage high-grade EC, 7%12% for early-stage CCC and 30% for infiltrative mucinous ovarian cancer. Randomised stage I-II tubo-ovarian carcinoma trials found longer survival with adjuvant platinum-based ChT but did not prospectively assess histological subtypes. High-grade EC prognosis resembles HGSC and is worse than low-grade EC. Whether adjuvant ChT improves survival in stage IA or IB CCC is unclear. Recommendation 7.1 [IV, A]: Standard surgery for stage I-II high-grade EC, CCC and high-risk mucinous ovarian carcinoma should fully resect disease and include total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingooophorectomy, omentectomy, systematic pelvic and paraaortic lymph-node dissection, peritoneal biopsies and cytology; consensus 97% (38) yes, 3% (1) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 7.2 [IV, A]: Offer adjuvant platinum-based ChT for stage I-II high-grade EC; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 7.3 [IV, C]: Adjuvant ChT may be omitted after adequate staging of IA or IB CCC; consensus 90% (35) yes, 5% (2) no, 5% (2) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 7.4 [IV, C]: Consider adjuvant ChT in stage IC1 CCC; consensus 92% (36) yes, 8% (3) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 7.5 [IV, A]: Give adjuvant ChT for stages IC2, IC3 and II CCC; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 7.6 [IV, A]: Offer adjuvant platinum-based ChT for high-risk stage I-II mucinous ovarian carcinoma; consensus 97% (38) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters).

document_sections.heading: 8. How should ovarian SBTs with peritoneal implants be managed?
document_sections.content: Ovarian SBT is a proliferative, low-grade serous epithelial neoplasm without invasion. Extraovarian peritoneal implants occur in 14%-30% of SBTs. The 2020 World Health Organization classification separates invasive from non-invasive implants. Invasive implants generally have a predominant epithelial component, often with a micropapillary/cribriform pattern and retraction artefact, together with destructive invasion of underlying tissue or replacement of normal omental architecture. Their prognosis is worse than that of non-invasive implants. Recommendation 8.1 [V, A]: Because implant pathology is complex, obtain expert pathological review; consensus 100% (41) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 8.2 [V, A]: Manage stage II-III ovarian SBT in a specialist centre; consensus 95.1% (39) yes, 2.4% (1) no, 2.4% (1) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 8.3 [IV, A]: Preserve the invasive versus non-invasive distinction when planning subsequent management; consensus 92% (36) yes, 5% (2) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 8.4 [V, A]: Resect peritoneal and omental disease to establish whether implants are invasive; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters).

document_sections.heading: 9. How should early-stage LGSC with non-invasive peritoneal implants be managed?
document_sections.content: Randomised evidence for ChT or hormonal treatment is lacking. LGSC is considerably less sensitive to ChT than HGSC, although most reports concern relapsed disease. A meta-analysis of retrospective studies reported occult nodal metastases in 2.9% of apparently early-stage, low-grade tubo-ovarian carcinoma. Recommendation 9.1 [IV, A]: Completely excise peritoneal implants and perform peritoneal staging as standard treatment; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 9.2 [IV, A]: Remove enlarged or suspicious nodes but do not routinely perform systematic lymphadenectomy; consensus 85% (33) yes, 15% (6) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 9.3 [IV, C]: Adjuvant ChT may be considered in stage II LGSC; consensus 92% (36) yes, 5% (2) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 9.4 [V, C]: Endocrine treatment following ChT may be considered for stage II LGSC; consensus 90% (35) yes, 8% (3) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters).

document_sections.heading: 10. How should incidental STIC or microscopic HGSC be managed?
document_sections.content: In BRCA-mut high-risk populations undergoing RRBSO, reported STIC detection varies from 0.4%-8.5% and is approximately 10-fold higher than in low-risk populations. ‘Microinvasive’ tubal HGSC lacks a precise definition. STIC with associated microscopic invasive HGSC may give rise to peritoneal HGSC and should therefore be managed as HGSC. SEE-FIM sampling is recommended for BRCA-mut carriers and those whose genetic predisposition is unknown; improved diagnostic criteria using p53 and ki-67 staining reveal lesions previously missed by conventional sampling. Following RRBSO, STIC is associated with greater subsequent peritoneal carcinoma risk, supporting peritoneal staging. Recommendation 10.1 [V, B]: Manage microscopic HGSC as HGSC; consensus 97% (38) yes, 3% (1) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 10.2 [IV, A]: Apply SEE-FIM to RRBSO specimens; consensus 85.4% (35) yes, 0% (0) no, 14.6% (6) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 10.3 [IV, A]: Apply SEE-FIM when endometrial, tubal, ovarian or peritoneal origin is uncertain; consensus 97% (38) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 10.4 [V, B]: Microscopic examination of the entire fimbriae in benign conditions is suggested; consensus 87% (34) yes, 3% (1) no, 10% (4) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 10.5 [II, A]: Stage the peritoneum in STIC; consensus 97% (38) yes, 3% (1) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 10.6 [III, B]: Undertake staging or restaging in STIC, preferably minimally invasively; consensus 92% (36) yes, 5% (2) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 10.7 [IV, A]: Consider hysterectomy in STIC, especially with gBRCA1-mut; consensus 82% (32) yes, 10% (4) no, 8% (3) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 10.8 [IV, B]: If the uterus remains in a patient with STIC and gBRCA1mut, sample the endometrium; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 10.9 [V, E]: Do not perform lymphadenectomy for STIC; consensus 95% (37) yes, 0% (0) no, 5% (2) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 10.10 [IV, D]: Do not give adjuvant ChT for surgically staged STIC; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 10.11 [II, A]: Testing for gBRCA1/2-muts and other high-penetrance hereditary genes is mandatory in STIC; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters).

document_sections.heading: Advanced stage (including older/frail patients)
document_sections.content: This topic covers selection for initial cytoreduction, HIPEC, maintenance therapy and care of older or frail patients. Detailed supporting evidence is identified in Supplementary Material Section 3.

document_sections.heading: 11. How should patients with advanced tubo-ovarian carcinoma be selected for primary cytoreductive surgery?
document_sections.content: Initial standard management is PCS, or NACT followed by ICS when upfront surgery is unsuitable. Randomised trials, despite limitations, found similar long-term survival and better perioperative outcomes with NACT than PCS, although PCS outcomes in those trials were unfavourable compared with other studies. Structured CT or diffusion-weighted MRI can help predict disease distribution, burden and resectability. PETeCT appears similarly accurate to CT for disease spread, possibly slightly better for nodal and distant metastases, but less reliable than diffusion-weighted MRI for intraperitoneal metastases. Centres meeting ESGO surgical and perioperative quality indicators support appropriate treatment. Prefer PCS where complete resection appears attainable with acceptable morbidity. LGSC requires different criteria: NACT is less effective than in HGSC; cytoreduction to <1 cm is preferable to no surgery, and the document reports significantly better PFS and OS with residual tumour 1 cm. A large phase III randomised trial failed to show therapeutic benefit from systematic lymphadenectomy after complete macroscopic peritoneal resection when nodes were not suspicious on preoperative imaging or intraoperative assessment; additional data found no benefit from comprehensive lymphadenectomy in advanced disease with rare histologies. Cardiophrenic nodes are an adverse prognostic factor, but survival effects of their removal are unknown. Recommendation 11.1 [IV, A]: An accredited ovarian cancer centre should select PCS versus NACT through multidisciplinary assessment under ESGO quality indicators for ovarian cancersurgery2016/2020; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 11.2 [I, A]: Prefer and offer PCS when complete resection appears achievable; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 11.3 [IV, B]: Prefer PCS for LGSC when residual disease <1 cm is achievable; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 11.4 [I, A]: NACT followed by ICS is an acceptable alternative when initial complete resection is unlikely and histology is chemosensitive, or medical conditions make surgery unsuitable; consensus 92% (36) yes, 5% (2) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 11.5 [IV, A]: A gynaecological oncology specialist should thoroughly assess surgical fitness against explicit criteria; obtain internal-medicine and/or anaesthesiology assessment if medically unfit and document Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group and American Society of Anesthesiology scores; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 11.6 [III, B]: For patients deemed surgical candidates by an MDT report, undertake laparotomy aiming for complete cytoreduction; consensus 97% (34) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (35 voters). Recommendation 11.7: Initial assessment options include contrast-enhanced CT, MRI and PETeCT with structured reporting [III, A]; expert US may assess pelvic and abdominal extent and resectability [III, C]; consensus 100% (35) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (35 voters). Recommendation 11.8 [IV, A]: Counsel patients on individual surgical benefits and risks, including a comprehensive account of possible major and minor perioperative complications; consensus 95% (37) yes, 3% (1) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 11.9 [III, B]: If structured imaging raises concern that cytoreduction will be incomplete, a gynaecological oncologist may assess intra-abdominal extent laparoscopically; consensus 92% (36) yes, 5% (2) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 11.10 [III, C]: Scoring systems may assist triage, but none is universally accepted for recommendation; consensus 90% (35) yes, 10% (4) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 11.11 [IV, C]: No specific biomarker currently validated predicts successful surgical resection; consensus 97% (38) yes, 3% (1) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 11.12 [I, E]: Do not undertake systematic pelvic and paraaortic lymphadenectomy after macroscopically complete intra-abdominal resection when nodes are not suspicious on imaging or operative evaluation; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 11.13 [IV, A]: Excise enlarged or suspicious nodes to obtain complete resection; consensus 100% (38) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (38 voters). Recommendation 11.14 [IV, C]: The benefit of removing suspicious or enlarged extra-abdominal nodes is uncertain; consider it when complete intra-abdominal macroscopic resection is achievable; consensus 95% (37) yes, 3% (1) no, 3% (1) abstain (39 voters). Recommendation 11.15 [IV, B]: Consider removing isolated liver parenchymal metastases to complete cytoreduction; consensus 100% (39) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (39 voters).

document_sections.heading: 12. What is the role of hyperthermic intraperitoneal ChT in newly diagnosed tubo-ovarian carcinoma?
document_sections.content: One prospective trial found better recurrence-free survival and OS when HIPEC was administered at ICS for FIGO stage III tubo-ovarian carcinoma. Its findings prompted substantial debate. The panel did not reach consensus on HIPEC with ICS, reflecting differing views.

document_sections.heading: 13. Which patients should receive bevacizumab, maintenance therapy with PARPis or the combination of PARPis with bevacizumab and for how long?
document_sections.content: Two randomised trials found a statistically significant PFS increase from adding bevacizumab to first-line paclitaxelecarboplatin and continuing it as maintenance versus ChT alone. Bevacizumab has activity across tubo-ovarian histotypes, including LGSC, and may be considered as maintenance for less-chemosensitive tumours. Most LGSCs have elevated estrogen and progesterone receptors; retrospective studies suggest possible maintenance benefit from hormonal treatment in newly diagnosed advanced LGSC. Up to 50% of HGSC is associated with HRD. Trials found significant PFS prolongation with PARPis, greatest in BRCA-mut tumours and next greatest in BRCA-wt HRD-positive tumours. Findings in BRCA-wt HRD-negative tumours are less conclusive: some trials report benefit and others no improvement. The document notes FDA and EMA approval of niraparib and EMA approval of rucaparib as maintenance monotherapy. Recommendation 13.1 [II, B]: Base maintenance choices on tumour molecular characteristics and patient- and disease-related factors; consensus 100% (36) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (36 voters). Recommendation 13.2 [I, A]: Recommend bevacizumab with ChT and as maintenance irrespective of biomarkers; consensus 89% (33) yes, 8% (3) no, 3% (1) abstain (37 voters). Recommendation 13.3 [I, A]: Combine bevacizumab with platinumepaclitaxel ChT and continue maintenance for a maximum of 15 months; consensus 97% (33) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (34 voters). Recommendation 13.4 [IV, A]: Treat carcinosarcoma as HGSC; consensus 100% (36) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (36 voters). Recommendation 13.5: Treat LGSC with paclitaxelecarboplatin ChT, with or without bevacizumab [II, A]; subsequent endocrine maintenance is an option for stage III and IV tumours [IV, B]; consensus 85.4% (35) yes, 12.2% (5) no, 2.4% (1) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 13.6 [I, A]: For HGSC/high-grade EC with BRCA-muts or validated-test GIS-positive status and CR/PR/NED after platinum-based ChT with or without bevacizumab, give PARPis with or without bevacizumab; consensus 100% (37) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (37 voters). Recommendation 13.7: For BRCA-mut-negative, validated-test GIS-negative HGSC/high-grade EC, options are platinum ChT plus bevacizumab followed by bevacizumab, or platinum ChT followed by niraparib or rucaparib if CR/PR/NED [I, B]; no maintenance may also be an option [I, C]; consensus 97% (36) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (37 voters). Recommendation 13.8 [I, B]: With no BRCA-mut and unknown GIS, options are platinum ChT plus bevacizumab followed by bevacizumab, or platinum ChT followed by niraparib or rucaparib after CR/PR/NED; consensus 97% (35) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (36 voters). Recommendation 13.9 [I, A]: Following CR/PR/NED on platinum ChT, use maintenance olaparib, alone or with bevacizumab, or rucaparib for 2 years; use niraparib for 3 years; consensus 97% (34) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (35 voters).

document_sections.heading: 14. How should older/frail patients with tubo-ovarian carcinoma be investigated and treated?
document_sections.content: Older people are under-represented in trials because of poor PS and comorbidities and have poorer outcomes. Geriatric assessment covers function, mental and nutritional state, emotional well-being and social support; trials have validated vulnerability scores. Surgery, often performed urgently outside specialist centres, is frequently incomplete and has more postoperative complications; ChT may be underused. Recommendation 14.1 [IV, D]: Do not exclude patients from diagnosis, trials or specific tubo-ovarian carcinoma treatment solely because of chronological age; consensus 100% (35) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (35 voters). Recommendation 14.2: Assess vulnerability in patients 70 years or of any age with at least two comorbidities, with geriatric specialist support if possible [IV, A]. Cover activities of daily living/instrumental activities of daily living, nutrition, psychological well-being, comorbidities and concomitant medicines [II, A], without delaying treatment [IV, A]; consensus 97% (35) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (36 voters). Recommendation 14.3 [III, B]: When feasible, recommend primary complete surgery after considering vulnerability, operative complexity and patient motivation; consensus 100% (36) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (36 voters). Recommendation 14.4 [III, B]: NACT may substitute for upfront surgery in vulnerable patients with extensive disease; consensus 97% (34) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (35 voters). Recommendation 14.5 [IV, A]: Perform surgery in expert centres with planned operations, pre-habilitation, intensive postoperative care, enhanced recovery and home care; consensus 97% (34) yes, 3% (1) no, 0% (0) abstain (35 voters). Recommendation 14.6: Standard ChT is paclitaxelecarboplatin every 3 weeks [I, A]; continuous weekly paclitaxel 60 mg/m2ecarboplatin AUC 2 may be better tolerated and improve QoL and can be considered instead [II, A]; consensus 92% (33) yes, 6% (2) no, 3% (1) abstain (36 voters). Recommendation 14.7 [II, A]: When indicated, offer PARPis and/or bevacizumab to older patients while closely monitoring toxicity and concomitant medications; consensus 97% (35) yes, 3% (1) no, 0% (0) abstain (36 voters).

document_sections.heading: Recurrent disease
document_sections.content: This topic covers surgery, molecularly targeted treatment, non-platinum options, supportive care and follow-up. Detailed supporting evidence is identified in Supplementary Material Section 4.

document_sections.heading: 15. What is the role of surgery in recurrent tubo-ovarian carcinoma?
document_sections.content: Surgery at recurrence aims at cytoreduction or palliation. Of three randomised trials at first relapse, two showed better PFS and one better OS with surgery versus no surgery. No prospective randomised evidence evaluates cytoreduction at later relapses; evidence for tertiary and quaternary procedures comes from a multicentre retrospective series. Palliation of bowel obstruction with disseminated peritoneal disease is difficult. When conservative medicines fail, possibilities include bypass, stoma, bowel decompression, endoscopic stents and percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy. Surgical morbidity is high and expert MDT input is crucial. OMD definitions depend on tumour and diagnostic method. Frequent sites include nodes, liver, spleen, lung, bone and brain; site independently influences prognosis. Surgery, infield RT and thermal ablation are used. Recommendation 15.1 [I, A]: At first recurrence >6 months after first-line platinum-based ChT, assess suitability for secondary cytoreduction in an experienced gynaecological oncology centre; consensus 100% (35) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (35 voters). Recommendation 15.2 [I, A]: Guide selection for complete secondary resection with prospectively validated algorithms; consensus 100% (35) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (35 voters). Recommendation 15.3 [IV, D]: Do not recommend NACT before recurrence cytoreduction outside clinical trials; consensus 75.6% (31) yes, 9.8% (4) no, 14.6% (6) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 15.4 [II, D]: Do not use HIPEC during cytoreduction for relapse; consensus 97% (33) yes, 3% (1) no, 0% (0) abstain (34 voters). Recommendation 15.5 [III, B]: Consider offering cytoreduction at subsequent relapses when complete resection appears possible; consensus 81% (29) yes, 8% (3) no, 11% (4) abstain (36 voters). Recommendation 15.6: Selected patients may need palliative tumour removal or diversion such as a stoma for mechanical obstruction after conservative management fails [IV, B]; manage them through an MDT [IV, A]; consensus 97.6% (40) yes, 0% (0) no, 2.4% (1) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 15.7 [IV, B]: Offer palliative surgery only after careful consideration when circumstances are unfavourable, including rapid progression without further systemic treatment, gastric outlet/upper gastrointestinal obstruction or obstruction at multiple levels; consensus 92.7% (38) yes, 4.9% (2) no, 2.4% (1) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 15.8 [IV, B]: Consider surgery, infield RT or thermal ablation for oligometastatic recurrence within an MDT; consensus 97% (34) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (35 voters). Recommendation 15.9 [IV, B]: Choose an oligometastatic treatment by recurrence location and timing, lesion number, treatment morbidity, PS, maintenance-treatment type and patient preference, irrespective of BRCA status; consensus 100% (34) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (34 voters). Recommendation 15.10 [IV, C]: Continuing the same maintenance regimen after local ablation or surgery may be considered; consensus 94% (32) yes, 3% (1) no, 3% (1) abstain (34 voters).

document_sections.heading: 16. What is the role of molecularly targeted therapy in recurrent disease?
document_sections.content: Selection of targeted therapy alongside platinum, currently bevacizumab or PARPis, depends on biology, previous targeted treatment and regulatory approvals. Adding bevacizumab to platinum ChT and continuing maintenance raises response rates and PFS without improving OS. In randomised recurrence trials, PARPis maintenance after platinum response significantly prolonged PFS until progression or intolerable toxicity; benefit was greatest with BRCA-mut but remained relevant in BRCA-wt regardless of HRD. Recurrent use is decreasing as first-line use increases. Later targeted treatment must account for first-line therapy. Retreatment with the same targeted drug remains experimental and lacks regulatory approval; further research is needed. Proactive maintenance monitoring helps manage adverse effects and sustain benefit. Recommendation 16.1: For platinum-eligible BRCA-mut disease without prior PARPis or bevacizumab, give platinum combination followed by PARPis after CR/PR/NED [I, A]; bevacizumab remains an option according to symptoms and ChT response [II, B]; consensus 94% (32) yes, 3% (1) no, 3% (1) abstain (34 voters). Recommendation 16.2 [I, A]: With platinum eligibility, BRCA-wt or unknown status and no prior PARPis or bevacizumab, recommend PARPis maintenance after CR/PR/NED or bevacizumab maintenance; prioritise bevacizumab with ChT followed by maintenance when rapid symptom control is needed; consensus 97% (34) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (35 voters). Recommendation 16.3 [I, A]: With platinum eligibility, earlier bevacizumab but no PARPis, prefer platinum ChT followed by PARPi maintenance after CR/PR/NED irrespective of BRCA or HRD; consensus 97% (30) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (31 voters). Recommendation 16.4 [I, A]: With platinum eligibility and earlier PARPis but not bevacizumab, recommend platinum combination plus bevacizumab and maintenance; prefer carboplatinepegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD) as bevacizumab's ChT partner at recurrence [I, A]; consensus 90% (27) yes, 3% (1) no, 7% (2) abstain (30 voters). Recommendation 16.5: With platinum eligibility and prior bevacizumab and PARPis, still recommend platinum ChT [I, B]; maintenance-agent rechallenge may be considered subject to recommendations 16.9 and 16.11; consensus 97% (29) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (30 voters). Recommendation 16.6 [I, A]: Monitor safety according to drug-specific guidance, particularly late-onset issues; consensus 100% (30) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (30 voters). Recommendation 16.7 [III, C]: Provide routine oncological follow-up using imaging and/or CA-125 according to local practice after patient discussion; consensus 97% (30) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (31 voters). Recommendation 16.8 [I, A]: Continue PARPis maintenance at recurrence until progression or unacceptable toxicity; consensus 100% (32) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (32 voters). Recommendation 16.9 [I, A]: Consider bevacizumab rechallenge with platinum after first-line bevacizumab; consensus 91% (29) yes, 6% (2) no, 3% (1) abstain (32 voters). Recommendation 16.10 [I, A]: Prefer carboplatinePLD as the ChT partner for bevacizumab rechallenge; consensus 97% (29) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (30 voters). Recommendation 16.11 [II, B]: After platinum response following earlier PARPi maintenance, PARPi maintenance rechallenge may be considered given prior exposure of 18 months in first line and 12 months in later lines, or 12 months and 6 months for BRCA-mut and BRCA-wt patients, respectively; consensus 94% (29) yes, 0% (0) no, 6% (2) abstain (31 voters).

document_sections.heading: 17. What is the role of non-platinum drugs and supportive care options?
document_sections.content: Non-platinum agents and supportive care chiefly serve patients unsuitable for platinum rechallenge because disease progressed on platinum or the TFI was short. Prognosis is poor, so symptom palliation and preserved QoL are principal aims. Non-platinum ChT may be used alone or with bevacizumab; endocrine therapy or trametinib is used for LGSC. Available treatments have limited efficacy, making trial participation important when feasible. No validated predictor identifies who benefits from palliative ChT. Low initial global health status, poor physical functioning and abdominal or gastrointestinal symptoms predict early discontinuation. Recommendation 17.1 [I, A]: If progression occurs on platinum or after a short TFI, or platinum is intolerable and rechallenge unsuitable, consider options from single-agent non-platinum systemic treatment to supportive care alone; consensus 97% (30) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (31 voters). Recommendation 17.2 [IV, A]: Enrol patients in trials when possible because better treatment options are substantially needed; consensus 100% (41) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (41 voters). Recommendation 17.3: Without previous bevacizumab, consider adding it to weekly paclitaxel, PLD or topotecan [I, A]; subset analysis favours weekly paclitaxel plus bevacizumab [II, A]; consensus 87% (26) yes, 3% (1) no, 10% (3) abstain (30 voters). Recommendation 17.4 [II, C]: Consider trabectedin with PLD for platinum-intolerant patients relapsing after 6 months from their last platinum dose; consensus 77% (24) yes, 16% (5) no, 6% (2) abstain (31 voters). Recommendation 17.5: At LGSC relapse after platinum failure, consider trametinib [I, A] or endocrine therapy [II, A]; consensus 97% (30) yes, 0% (0) no, 3% (1) abstain (31 voters). Recommendation 17.6 [III, A]: Consider supportive care alone if anticipated ChT benefit is limited; consensus 100% (30) yes, 0% (0) no, 0% (0) abstain (30 voters). Recommendation 17.7 [III, A]: Assess QoL and symptoms systematically during treatment to initiate supportive care early and prevent or improve symptoms, QoL and survival; consensus 88% (28) yes, 9% (3) no, 3% (1) abstain (32 voters).

document_sections.heading: 18. What is recommended regarding evaluation of QoL/ survivorship issues and follow-up after treatment?
document_sections.content: Symptoms due to treatment or tumour are often underestimated and may persist during treatment and follow-up. Assess symptoms and QoL as early as possible and provide access to early supportive services, which may improve symptoms, QoL and survival; these include psycho-oncology, social care, physiotherapy and patient support groups. Oncological follow-up seeks recurrence or secondary cancers, monitors QoL, addresses treatment-related toxicity and supplies holistic support. No follow-up schedule or protocol is standard. A reasonable approach is assessment every 34 months for the first 2 years and every 6 months in years 3-5; individualise according to prognostic factors and treatments such as maintenance, and discuss follow-up beyond 5 years individually. Recommendation 18.1 [IV, C]: Consider validated QoL and symptom instruments during routine follow-up for all ovarian carcinoma patients; consensus 96% (26) yes, 0% (0) no, 4% (1) abstain (27 voters). Recommendation 18.2 [III, A]: Arrange long-term follow-up for all tubo-ovarian carcinoma patients with a physician experienced in gynaecological cancer treatment and follow-up; consensus 90% (27) yes, 10% (3) no, 0% (0) abstain (30 voters).
